background.definition: Torticollis, also known as cervical dystonia or "wry neck." It is a condition that involves spasm of the neck muscles which results in involuntary rotation of the cervical spine and is frequently associated with pain. The condition can be congenital, idiopathic, or a secondary phenomenon caused by an underlying pathology.

list.listitem: 9 per 100,000 yearly.
1 per 250 live births.
Presentation in infancy is frequently associated with a sternocleidomastoid or other neck musculature mass.
Adult presentations can be considered primary (hereditary conditions or idiopathic) or secondary (trauma, metabolic, infectious, drug induced, and neurological).
Consider drug-induced causes, including antianxiety agents, antiemetics, neuroleptics, anticonvulsants, lithium, and antidepressants.
Consider trauma to the cervical spine and cranial injury.
In children following head and neck surgery, consider atlantoaxial non-traumatic subluxation (Grisel syndrome).
Infectious meningitis or abscess of the head or neck can cause spasm to neck musculature.
Neurological (all rare) causes include Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, Wilson's disease, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, Leigh's disease, and Niemann-Pick disease.
Cervical dystonia appears to be caused by neurochemical abnormities in the basal ganglia and possibly the cerebellum.

list.listitem: Suspect torticollis in a patient with involuntary posturing of the head or persistent spasm of the neck musculature. C
A thorough history and physical are warranted in all cases of torticollis to look for underlying primary causes. C
Tailor further diagnostic evaluation if an underlying primary cause is suspected (patient with signs of mass, infection, or trauma). C
Patients with torticollis present with an involuntary posturing of the neck. While the presentation can involve symptoms of pain, pain does not have to be present for the diagnosis to be made.

Diagnosis is directed at determining the cause of the symptom, which may be either idiopathic or a reaction to underlying primary pathology. Obtain a thorough history documenting timing of symptoms and intensity of pain or spasm; also document whether pain is exacerbating or stable, whether any measures have been taken to help the symptoms, and whether these were effective.

The history should determine the chronicity of the condition; if acute, this may indicate a serious infectious etiology such as meningitis or retropharyngeal abscess that presents with torticollis as a symptom. A history of recent fever, malaise, focal or generalized pain, palpable mass of the neck, neck stiffness, falls, or direct trauma to the head, neck, or spine should be considered a "red flag" for underlying primary etiology.

Physical examination should focus directly on eliminating underlying primary causes for the condition; retropharyngeal abscess; meningitis; mass or tumor in the neck musculature or brain; underlying soft tissue abscess; head, spine, or neck trauma or evidence of injury; cervical spine pathology; mastoiditis, pharyngeal or dental pathology; or otic pathology.

To further characterize torticollis, the Movement Disorders Society recommends several scales including the Cervical Dystonia Impact Scale, the Toronto Western Spasmodic Torticollis Rating Scale, the Craniocervical Dystonia Questionnaire, and the Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale for rating generalized dystonia.

Authors from the Radiological Society of North America recommend ultrasound to investigate torticollis in newborns or infants with suspected congenital torticollis. In cases of secondary torticollis from trauma, plain films (lateral and anteroposterior views) are recommended as initial imaging modality. In nontraumatic acquired torticollis, computed tomography (CT) of the neck or cervical spine is recommended with magnetic resonance imaging if CT findings are negative.
Patients with palpable neck mass need imaging. (ultrasound if child, ultrasound or CT if adult).
Patients who are acutely ill or have signs and symptoms consistent with abscess or meningitis need lumbar puncture and possibly imaging.
Consider conservative therapy initially (NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, rest, massage); consider botulinum toxin if symptoms persist.
Treatment is directed at the specific etiology of torticollis, which emphasizes the need for an accurate diagnosis. B
NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, manual medicine techniques such as osteopathic manipulative treatment, and massage are commonly recommended for conservative therapy, but good clinical trials are lacking. C
Botulinum toxin A (BTA) injections A and botulinum toxin B (BTB) injections B are effective but are not needed for all patients.
NSAIDs and muscle relaxants are often recommended, but clinical trials are lacking for these drugs in patients with torticollis.

Both BTA and BTB have similar clinical benefits; BTA possibly has a longer duration of action and marginally better side effect profile. Polymyographic electromyography can be considered for selecting the dystonic muscles for treatment with BTA/B as clinical examination does not always identify the muscles involved and one study found significantly improved outcome of botulinum toxin treatment using this approach.
The American Academy of Neurology states that BTA and BTB are beneficial in adult cervical dystonia and should be offered.
Botulinum toxin is superior to placebo for spasmodic torticullis.
A single study comparing botulinum toxin A therapy with trihexyphenidyl for the treatment of cervical dystonia found greater efficacy with botulinum toxin.
Surgery is indicated for patients with torticollis secondary to operable pathology.
Physiotherapy, relaxation therapy, and EMG feedback have been recommended.
In one case series, outcomes in 50 young infants with congenital muscular torticollis following physiotherapy were good despite the presence of severe fibrosis on ultrasound.

Predictors of 65 mothers' adherence to physical therapy for their infants with congenital torticollis were maternal perceptions of torticollis effect on her infant's activities and the program's importance for the infant's future function.
Case studies looking at osteopathic manipulative treatment have shown permanent resolution of symptoms, however, more substantial research is needed to improve the quality of evidence.
For children with atlantoaxial non-traumatic subluxation manual repositioning and temporary immobilization with a cervical collar for 2 weeks can also be considered based on a case report.

Authors of a case series of 8 patients reported good outcomes (reduced severity, pain and disability) at follow-up following deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus. In a randomized cross-over trial of 12 patients with refractory dystonia, deep brain stimulation of either the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus internus improved the Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale and quality of life physical scores at 6 months.

Hospitalization should be considered for any patient with cervical dystonia symptoms thought to be of an infectious or traumatic etiology, a potential threat to respiratory status, or for those patients who are experiencing intractable pain.

Younger age at onset is the only consistent clinical feature associated with remission. B In one trial, 31/37 infants, regardless of treatment group, achieved symmetric head posture before the age of 12 months.

Congenital muscular torticollis, however, was associated with a developmental delay or disorder (e.g., attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, developmental coordination disorder, language impairment, autistic spectrum disorder) in 30/68 (44.1%) of children in one follow-up study at age 7 to 9 years.
Remissions occurring in the first 2 years after onset in adults are typically not sustained. B
Treatment using BtA is associated with a 5% to 10% rate of developed resistance to BtA therapy. B

Treatment with BtB in cases of BtA resistance appears to be clinically effective for relief of symptoms, but long-term efficacy has not been established. One RCT non-inferiority trial found that both BtA and BtB were effective and safe for the treatment of toxin-naive subjects with cervical dystonia; duration of effect was similar (13.1 and 13.7 weeks, respectively). B
Ultrasound is the preferred imaging study in children due to lower radiation exposure.
There is an association between congenital muscular torticollis (CMT) and hip dysplasia.
In one case series, 5.5% of 292 children with CMT had hip dysplasia all of whom had an abnormal hip examination.
